question_hint: On the fraud model, you wrote 'heavy class imbalance—class weights over resampling after ablation.' Walk me through how you compared those approaches and why class weights won.
expected_points: Stated the business context and imbalance ratio (fraud was well under 1% of ~40M transactions) and why PR/recall-at-precision was the guiding metric, not accuracy or ROC AUC.
Benchmarked random undersampling, SMOTE, and class weighting under identical XGBoost settings and the same temporal validation, measuring PR AUC and recall at 90% precision.
Explained tradeoffs: resampling changes the training distribution and can overfit to synthetic/duplicated examples; class weights are a single knob and preserve real data.
Noted class weights only change the training loss, so the final decision threshold was tuned afterward on the validation PR curve.
Quantified the offline result: recall improved to 0.62 at 90% precision from a 0.41 baseline.

question_hint: You said TimeSeriesSplit prevented leakage. What leakage would happen with random splitting on transaction data, and how exactly did you construct your train/test splits?
expected_points: Identified entity leakage: a random split puts the same card or merchant in both train and test, letting the model memorize accounts instead of generalizing.
Identified time/feature leakage: aggregations or labels that span the prediction date make the past look like the future; features must be computed as-of the transaction timestamp.
Split by transaction timestamp into expanding or purged folds, with a gap/embargo between train and test to handle delayed fraud labels and rolling aggregates.
Tuned hyperparameters only on the training folds and saved a final holdout (e.g., the most recent weeks or months) for unbiased evaluation.

question_hint: How did you arrive at that 90%-precision operating point, and what did the fraud operations team sign off on?
expected_points: Mapped precision to cost per review or false positive and recall to expected fraud loss; set the threshold from the PR curve where the marginal cost of review equaled the expected fraud avoided.
Evaluated candidate thresholds on the validation PR curve and compared to the previous model's operating point, which had recall 0.41 at the same precision.
Acknowledged the tradeoff: at 90% precision the model sacrifices recall on roughly 38% of fraud but keeps the review queue manageable.
Mentioned that model scores are not necessarily calibrated, so the threshold was treated as a business decision rather than a statistical default like 0.5.

question_hint: Walk me through your canary rollout: how did you decide it was safe to send more traffic, and what exactly would trigger a rollback?
expected_points: Staged traffic in small increments (e.g., 5% to 25% to 100% of eligible transactions) through the versioned model registry and the FastAPI service on Kubernetes.
Monitored health and consistency gates: request error rate, p99 latency, model score distribution, PSI versus the champion model, and downstream review or decline rates.
Rolled back by repointing the model registry tag or service selector to the previous model version—well under the stated five-minute target.
Distinguished canary testing from A/B business evaluation: canary catches system breakages and gross distribution shifts, while offline-to-online business lift needs a separate experiment.

question_hint: You built drift monitoring with PSI > 0.2 and a five-minute rollback. What does a PSI alert actually tell you, and what do you do with it?
expected_points: Defined PSI as sum of (actual percentage - expected percentage) * ln(actual percentage / expected percentage), usually computed per feature and on the model score over a rolling window.
Explained that a PSI alert signals covariate shift but not the cause or whether performance actually degraded; it could be a legit seasonal change or an upstream data pipeline bug.
Paired PSI with decision-rate and outcome monitoring, since fraud labels arrive late and accuracy cannot be tracked in real time.
Used rollback as a safety valve while investigating root cause, then decided whether retraining was appropriate or whether the data-quality issue needed fixing upstream.

question_hint: P99 went from 180 ms to 45 ms. How did you find that bottleneck, and why was Redis plus batching the right fix?
expected_points: Profiled p50 and p99 separately and found the bottleneck was many per-request feature lookups and network round trips, not the XGBoost tree scoring itself.
Precomputed as-of features into Redis with TTL and versioning so the serving path fetches them with a single mget or pipeline instead of expensive warehouse joins per call.
Batched model calls and feature lookups, often with async concurrency, to amortize network and native-library overhead at production QPS.
Considered simple local caching but rejected it because stateless replicas would go stale or miss updates; Redis added an infrastructure dependency and required cache-refresh jobs.
Verified the change with load tests at production traffic, confirming the p99 drop to 45 ms without changing model inputs or accuracy.

question_hint: Your resume centers on offline precision/recall. How did you verify the new model actually moved business metrics once it was live?
expected_points: Defined business success metrics before shipping—fraud loss rate, false positive or review rate, decline or approval rate, and chargeback rate—not just offline AUC.
Ran a shadow-mode or A/B comparison with logged model scores and delayed outcomes, comparing the new model against the incumbent on live traffic.

Computed realized precision and recall under the production threshold, accounting for label delay and intervention bias because reviewed or declined transactions never receive a clean ground-truth label.
Worked with product and data engineering to size the experiment and read out the business lift, acknowledging that offline gains can shrink when fraud patterns shift post-deployment.

topic: Retraining triggers and production data quality
question_hint: Mid-level engineers here own monitoring and retraining. What event convinced you to retrain, and what production data-quality issue did you hit along the way?
expected_points: Had explicit retraining triggers: a scheduled cadence or a combination of drift and performance alerts, rather than retraining blindly on every data shift.

Described a representative data-quality incident—for example, an upstream schema change, a feature returning null or a default value, or timestamps shifting timezones—that initially looked like model drift.
Investigated with data validation, versioned feature definitions, and checks of whether the distribution shift was real or caused by a pipeline bug before deciding to retrain.
Retrained through a champion-challenger process in CI with regression gates, then deployed via canary, keeping the previous artifact in the model registry for rollback.

question_hint: Before building, how did you define the problem and decide on the target metric? Walk me through the tradeoff between recall and precision for this fraud use case.
expected_points: Framed as a binary classification problem but explicitly tied to fraud loss, review cost, and customer friction; not just accuracy.
Targeted high precision as the constraint to avoid blocking legitimate transactions; recall 0.62 at 90% precision was a concrete operating point.
Chose PR-AUC / PR curve over ROC due to extreme class imbalance; precision/recall more informative than false positive rate.
Mentioned alternatives: e.g., tuning threshold vs. changing model objective; also considered cost-sensitive learning aligned to dollar loss.
Stated business metric such as fraud loss avoided, false positive rate budget, or dollars saved from the previous model

topic: Validation strategy: TimeSeriesSplit and leakage prevention
question_hint: You mentioned using TimeSeriesSplit. Walk me through the exact train/validation split — how did you prevent leakage across time, and what leakage risks were you worried about?
expected_points: Used TimeSeriesSplit with training data strictly before validation data in time to respect the temporal order of fraud labeling and feature computation.
Identified key leak vectors: transaction features computed with future information (e.g., labels from chargebacks that arrive after the prediction timestamp) and oversampling before splitting.
Ensured feature engineering used only information available at prediction time: no future aggregations, no target encoding with full data, no global scaling fit on test.
Explained why random K-fold would overestimate performance: fraud patterns shift and same user/merchant transactions can appear across folds.
Maybe mentioned purging/embargo or gap between train and test to account for delayed labels.

topic: Class imbalance: class weights vs resampling
question_hint: You wrote you used class weights over resampling after ablation. Can you walk me through that experiment — what did you compare, and why did class weights win?
expected_points: Described comparison types: no weighting, class_weight='balanced' or manual weights, random undersampling of majority, SMOTE/oversampling of minority, possibly ensemble of undersampled models.
Evaluated each with the same PR curve / thresholding and TimeSeriesSplit; class weights gave better recall@precision on out-of-time validation than resampling.
Class weights are simpler and avoid generating synthetic fraud transactions (SMOTE) that don't match real fraud dynamics and can leak across time.
Fitted class weights only on training folds and applied proportional weights; did not tune them heavily on the test set.
Mentioned the practical production benefit: simpler pipeline, faster training, easy to serve, less risk of overfitting noisy minority examples.

question_hint: How did you choose the 90% precision operating point? What was the process after training to set the threshold, and how did it hold up in production?
expected_points: Threshold was selected on validation PR curve by finding the recall at the desired precision (90%) and translating that score threshold to a decision rule.
Balanced false-positive cost (review cost and customer friction) against fraud loss; likely simulated dollar cost using an expected value calculation.
Explained that choosing the threshold offline is only step one; online results were tracked via A/B test or shadow mode, and threshold adjusted if business metric shifted.
Discussed the performance gain: recall 0.62 at 90% precision, up from 0.41 — probably compared to the previous production model; this justified moving forward.
Mentioned that threshold tuning on PR curves is more robust than ROC to class imbalance and does not imply calibration; also considered probability calibration if needed.

question_hint: Take me through the rollout. How exactly did you do the canary deployment on Kubernetes, and what made a new model version safe to promote?
expected_points: Served model behind FastAPI in a Kubernetes Deployment; used a versioned model registry (e.g., S3/SageMaker or MLflow) to fetch specific model artifacts.
Canary rollout: routed small % of live traffic to new model pod, monitored KPIs (fraud detection rate, false positive rate, latency, errors), then increased traffic if metrics stayed green.
Defined rollback criteria and practiced rollback — versioned registry allowed switch back in under 5 minutes by changing the active model pointer.
Described integration with feature store: real-time features served from Redis; no data pipeline dependency at request time.
A/B or shadow-mode evaluation compared new model to old on live traffic before full promotion; business metric movement was tracked, not just offline AUC.

question_hint: You mentioned feature drift monitoring with PSI > 0.2. Concretely, how was that computed, what did you do when it tripped, and did you confuse drift with data-quality issues?
expected_points: Computed PSI on feature distributions between a reference window (e.g., last 30 days of training data) and a current production window; PSI > 0.2 triggered an alert.
Had alerting on both per-feature and model score PSI, plus a dashboard to slice by feature, segment, or time to root cause.
When PSI tripped, first checked for data pipeline bugs (feature nulls, unit changes, schema mismatches, timestamp issues) before assuming real concept drift.
Had runbook: assess severity, compare recent label/chargeback feedback if available, decide to retrain, add feature monitoring, or rollback to a more stable model.
Mentioned limitation: PSI monitors features, not model performance; labels arrive late in fraud so used delayed label analysis and a holdout to catch degradation.

topic: Latency optimization: Redis feature store and batching
question_hint: Explain how you cut p99 from 180 ms to 45 ms. What did you optimize, and what tradeoffs did that introduce for feature consistency or model accuracy?
expected_points: Identified bottleneck: feature lookups to remote DB / compute inside request path; moved precomputed features to Redis for O(1) reads.
Added batching for model inference (e.g., batching multiple transactions in a single request or using batched inference inside the service) to reduce per-request overhead.
Optimized feature engineering code, process warmup, protobuf/serialization, or kept model artifact small/quantized? They need to be concrete about what they changed.
Discussed tradeoff: features in Redis may be stale compared to recomputing on the fly; so they set TTL and invalidation strategy, accepted minor staleness in exchange for low latency.
Measured the impact with load tests and production p99; monitored error rate and drift; verified latency reduction did not change model predictions relative to original feature values.

topic: Model lifecycle in production: retraining and A/B evaluation
question_hint: After you shipped, how did you handle retraining? What triggers a retraining cycle, and how do you evaluate a new candidate model against the current one in production?
expected_points: Described scheduled retraining (e.g., daily/weekly) plus event-driven retraining on drift or performance decline.
Described an A/B or champion-challenger setup: new candidate trained on updated data is evaluated offline first on recent time windows, then served shadow or small canary.
Used business-focused success metrics (fraud prevented, false positive rate, customer impact) and statistical significance; not just offline AUC/PR.
Handled delayed labels: computed actual fraud on older transactions to measure performance; for near-real-time decisions, used incremental proxy metrics like chargeback rate.
Mentioned tradeoff between frequent retraining (cost, pipeline complexity, risk of overfitting to recent concept drift) and stability; monitored and rolled back automatically when needed.

question_hint: Let's go deep on retrieval. Walk me through why you chose BM25 plus embeddings over either alone — and what measured evidence drove that choice.
expected_points: Built a golden set of real support questions with labeled relevant docs/chunks before deciding on a retrieval strategy.
Compared BM25-only, embedding-only, and hybrid on Recall@5; hybrid clearly outperformed either single retriever because it captured exact terms and paraphrases.
Combined normalized BM25 and embedding scores with weighted fusion or reciprocal rank fusion, then tuned the fusion weights on the golden set.
Retrieval decisions were validated by downstream metrics like groundedness, not by eyeballing examples.
Learned that retrieval is a set of tunable parameters that must be measured against a labeled evaluation set first.

question_hint: How did you handle chunking and embedding for 12k internal docs, and how did you validate that it worked beyond a gut check?
expected_points: Tested a few chunk-size and overlap settings and evaluated each configuration with Recall@5 on the golden set rather than relying on intuition.
Preferred structure-aware chunks aligned with document headings/sections, and added overlap or joined paragraphs where answers were likely to span chunk boundaries.
Picked an embedding model by running retrieval experiments on representative internal docs, not just on public benchmarks.
Included metadata like doc title/source in each chunk to support later citation and debugging.
Even after chunking looked good, re-checked answer groundedness because good retrieval is only a means to faithful answers.

question_hint: Tell me about the reranking stage: what did you use, and what did it actually change in the final system?
expected_points: Used a cross-encoder reranker over the shortlist produced by BM25 + embedding retrieval.
Retrieved roughly 20 candidates, reranked them, and passed only the top 3-5 chunks to the LLM to keep the prompt focused.
Measured the reranker's impact on Recall@k and on LLM-judge groundedness; it produced a meaningful lift over the fused retrieval alone.
Accepted the extra reranking latency because the support assistant valued answer precision and groundedness over a few extra milliseconds.
Without reranking, relevant-but-lexically-different chunks sometimes ranked too low; reranking fixed those ordering errors.

question_hint: You claimed 89% grounded. How was that number produced, and what did you actually do with it?
expected_points: Built an LLM-as-judge prompt that compares each generated claim against the retrieved chunks and outputs grounded or not-grounded with a short reason.
Before trusting the judge, validated it against human annotations and iterated on the rubric until agreement was high enough.
The 89% figure was the answer-faithfulness/groundedness rate on a fixed evaluation set after the final prompt and retrieval tuning.
Used this metric as the core regression gate and as the signal for deciding between prompt variants and retrieval configurations.
Also designed an explicit abstain/no-answer path when the LLM could not find support in the retrieved context, so low support did not force a hallucinated answer.

question_hint: You mentioned fine-tuning a small classifier to route tickets. What was the routing goal, and why distill from an LLM instead of just prompting the LLM every time?
expected_points: The router decided which tickets should go to the full retrieval-augmented generation path versus a cheaper path or human escalation, reducing overall cost and latency.
Used an LLM to label a sample of historical tickets, then fine-tuned a small classifier to imitate those labels; it achieved F1 0.87 on a holdout set.
The distilled classifier cost roughly 1/100th of the serving cost of the LLM labeler while preserving most routing accuracy.
Considered using the prompt-based LLM directly for routing but measured that it was too slow and expensive for the ticket volume.
Learned that task-specific small models can replace an LLM at the highest-volume, lowest-complexity part of a system.

topic: Offline evaluation harness and CI gates
question_hint: What exactly was in your offline evaluation harness, and how did you keep CI regression gates from being flaky or useless?
expected_points: Built golden sets from real support questions with labeled relevant documents and expected behaviors, not hand-written toy examples.
Ran deterministic retrieval metrics like Recall@5, plus LLM-judge groundedness for final answers and F1 for the route classifier.
Set the CI regression gate to fail a branch if a metric dropped more than a threshold relative to the baseline on the same golden set.
Pinned model versions and used temperature 0 with fixed ordering so comparisons were reproducible and not noisy.
Treated the golden set as a living artifact: every real failure or edge case found in production was added to it.

question_hint: When you put an LLM feature in front of real users, what do you worry about most and how do you protect against it?
expected_points: Most worried about hallucinated or ungrounded answers, especially when the answer sounds confident but was not in the retrieved context.
Mitigated by strict grounding instructions, requiring an abstain answer when context does not support the claim, and surfacing citations.
Tracked retrieval failure signals like empty retrieval results or low top-score margins to detect knowledge gaps.
Sampled production traffic and scored it with the same offline LLM judge to catch quality drift over time.
Built fallback paths so edge cases go to a human or a more deterministic process instead of forcing an unreliable LLM answer.

question_hint: Walk me through one explicit cost/latency/quality tradeoff you made. How did you decide the right operating point?
expected_points: Used the cheap distilled router to send the majority of simple tickets down a low-cost path and reserved expensive LLM/RAG calls for complex cases.
Evaluated smaller/cheaper LLM options on the golden set with the groundedness metric before swapping, rather than choosing based on model benchmarks.
Limited reranking and context size to what improved measurable answer quality without blowing the latency budget.
Monitored p95 latency, token spend per request, and groundedness over time to catch regressions early.
The guiding principle was always: make the change, measure quality with the eval harness, and roll back if the metric moved the wrong way.

question_hint: Walk me through the architecture of the support assistant at Corvid Analytics at a high level. What was your role, and what was the first major design decision you made?
expected_points: Described end-to-end flow: incoming question -> ticket router (fine-tuned classifier) -> BM25 + embedding hybrid retrieval over ~12k internal docs -> reranking -> grounded prompt -> answer with citations/sources.
Clarified personal ownership: retrieval stack, evaluation harness, and router/serving design; acknowledged collaboration on labeling and product integration.
First major design decision: choosing hybrid retrieval plus reranking instead of a single vector search, based on offline Recall@5 experiments on a golden set.
Set explicit quality targets from product requirements (answer grounded in evidence) and used those targets to drive all component choices.
Quoted the headline metric (89% grounded by an LLM judge) and explained how the architecture made that metric measurable and achievable.

topic: Retrieval design: chunking, embeddings, and hybrid search
question_hint: You mentioned hybrid retrieval over 12k docs. How did you decide on chunking and the specific mix of BM25 and embeddings? What did you measure to validate those choices?
expected_points: Compared chunking strategies — fixed token windows, paragraph-based, and heading-aware sections — using Recall@5 on a golden set; chose a chunk size that preserved context without fragmenting key sections.
Evaluated multiple embedding models or APIs on the same test set rather than defaulting to the largest one; weighed embedding dimension, cost, and retrieval quality.
Tuned the BM25/embedding fusion weights or rank-fusion method on validation data, not by intuition; found BM25 was essential for exact identifiers like product codes and error IDs.

Reported measured retrieval quality, including Recall@5 and how often the top chunks contained enough context for the generator; identified that most failures were recall failures, not ranking failures.
Discussed tradeoffs: larger chunks provided better context but diluted embeddings and increased reranker/generation token cost; final choice balanced those constraints.

question_hint: You mentioned adding reranking after hybrid retrieval. Which reranker did you use or compare, what latency did it add, and how did you justify keeping it?
expected_points: Used a cross-encoder reranker over the top-N candidates from hybrid retrieval (e.g., top 20-30) to keep reranking cost bounded.
Measured p95 latency before and after adding the reranker; quoted the added latency and confirmed it stayed within the product's end-to-end budget.
Ran an ablation: reranking improved the grounded-answer rate or downstream answer quality measurably, so it was worth the extra cost.
Considered alternatives like increasing top-k without reranking or using an LLM-as-reranker, and rejected them due to higher generation cost or worse quality/latency tradeoff.
Tuned reranker candidate pool size and top-k to balance recall and precision; evaluated with the CI eval harness rather than ad hoc samples.

topic: Grounded prompting and LLM-judge faithfulness measurement
question_hint: You said answer faithfulness was measured with an LLM judge and hit 89% grounded. What exactly did the judge check, and how did you engineer the prompt or context to keep answers grounded?
expected_points: Defined groundedness concretely: every factual claim in the answer must be supported by the retrieved passages; ungrounded statements or hallucinations counted as failures.

Designed the LLM judge prompt with the answer and source passages, requiring a structured verdict (e.g., grounded/partially grounded/ungrounded or per-sentence labels), and validated judge outputs against human annotations.
Engineered the generator prompt to answer only from the provided context, cite source chunks, and explicitly say when information was not found rather than guess.
Iterated on context formatting, instruction phrasing, and the number of retrieved chunks, measuring groundedness changes through the harness until reaching the 89% target.
Acknowledged LLM-judge caveats: prompt sensitivity and self-agreement issues, and added spot-checking or disagreement analysis to prevent the judge from becoming a blind spot.

topic: Evaluation harness and regression gates in CI
question_hint: You built offline eval harnesses with golden sets, Recall@5, and CI regression gates. How did you make those gates trustworthy enough to block releases, and what were their known failure modes?
expected_points: Constructed golden sets from real support tickets with human-annotated relevant passage IDs and reference answers; split them into dev and test sets to avoid overfitting thresholds.
Tracked multiple metrics: Recall@5 for retrieval and end-to-end metrics like groundedness/faithfulness and answer relevance; reported concrete values and thresholds.
Set regression gate thresholds from baseline noise rather than arbitrary values; a candidate change failed if relevant metrics dropped more than the measured variance.
Fought test-set contamination and data leakage by keeping golden queries disjoint from the indexed documents and updating goldens as documentation evolved.
Was explicit about limitations: offline metrics correlate imperfectly with production user satisfaction, so gates were paired with shadow traffic and human review of sampled outputs.

topic: Routing classifier and distillation cost tradeoff
question_hint: You fine-tuned a small classifier to route tickets and distilled it from an LLM labeler at 1/100th serving cost. Why was this routing step needed, and how did you evaluate the cost/quality tradeoff?
expected_points: Clarified that the router decided whether a query should go to the full RAG pipeline, a lighter path, or an escalation, avoiding unnecessary LLM calls for simple issues.
Reported the classifier's measured quality, e.g., F1 0.87 on a held-out routing test set, with the label taxonomy and example counts.
Explained the distillation process: an LLM generated labels on a large unlabeled corpus, then a small encoder model was fine-tuned on those labels; compared student F1 to the teacher's agreement.
Quantified cost/latency gains: the small model served at roughly 1/100th the LLM serving cost and added only a few milliseconds, making the tradeoff obviously worthwhile.
Discussed alternatives considered, such as using the LLM itself for routing with structured outputs, and why deterministic classification plus fallback to RAG was chosen in production.

topic: Production rollout, monitoring, and failure modes
question_hint: Once the assistant shipped, how did you monitor answer quality in production? What kind of bad behavior broke after launch, and how did you handle it?
expected_points: Put tracing and logging in place for queries, retrieved chunks, generated answers, and any user feedback; set up dashboards for p95 latency, cost per query, and groundedness judge pass rate on production samples.
Monitored retrieval health signals such as fraction of queries returning no results, low top scores, and rapid distribution shifts in query text or document updates.

Described a concrete post-launch issue, e.g., a doc re-index changed embedding distributions and hurt retrieval, or the generator produced fluent but partially ungrounded answers on edge cases; showed how monitoring caught it.
Used canary rollouts, versioned indexes, or a model/retrieval registry to revert a bad change quickly; tied incident response back to the eval harness.
Balanced offline 'groundedness' against real-world user satisfaction; discussed how feedback signals or downstream resolution data were used to adjust the quality thresholds.

question_hint: Stepping back: how did you budget cost and latency across retrieval, reranking, and generation in that project, and if you were redesigning it today with current tools, what would you change?
expected_points: Gave a clear latency budget: for example, p95 end-to-end target split across retrieval, rerank, and generation, with conscious decisions on top-k, reranker size, and model choice.
Used cost levers including the routing classifier, distillation, response caching for common queries, and a smaller/faster generation model for straightforward tickets.

Described a tradeoff framework: evaluate quality changes first with the harness, then compute the marginal cost per additional quality point; avoided optimizations that did not move user-facing metrics.
Would redesign by adding an explicit guardrails module for off-topic or unsafe inputs, better metadata filtering during retrieval, or incorporating user feedback more directly into the eval loop.
Stated a key lesson: LLM application behavior must be treated as measurable, and the evaluation harness is the backbone for making cost/latency/quality decisions safely.

question_hint: Sticking with the fraud model — how did you turn the ambiguous request 'build us a fraud model' into a well-defined ML problem? What exactly were you predicting, and whose decision did it influence?
expected_points: Clarified the decision: whether to review or block a card transaction in real-time, balancing fraud loss against false-positive cost and fraud-ops review workload.
Defined the target as confirmed fraud (e.g., chargeback/dispute) within a fixed outcome window, and explicitly handled time-to-label lag rather than using instant provisional labels.
Framed it as a per-transaction classification at authorization time, not a user/merchant-level model, because the product required a score in under ~200ms.
Set success in business terms — dollars of fraud prevented minus operational cost and false-positive friction — not just accuracy/AUC.
Made an explicit decision that the model output would be a threshold-tunable score, not a fixed auto-decline, to allow different operating points.

question_hint: You listed TimeSeriesSplit as a guard against leakage. Walk me through a specific way leakage could have sneaked into this fraud model and how your pipeline prevented it.
expected_points: Called out that features built from future information—like a customer aggregating all transactions up to next week—would leak; features used only data available at prediction time.
Identified label leakage: fraud confirmation/chargeback can arrive days after the transaction, so you must avoid using the eventual outcome as a feature for that same transaction.
Described an expanding-window TimeSeriesSplit, never random shuffled rows; trained on earlier months and validated on a later calendar month.
Mentioned an embargo/gap period between train and validation to account for outcome lag and prevent repeated/overlapping transactions across folds.
Verified no overlapping customers or cards across a fold's train and validation if those entities were in both due to repeat transactions.

topic: Class imbalance: class weights vs resampling
question_hint: You said you used class weights over resampling after ablation. What did the ablation compare, and why did class weights win?
expected_points: Compared random undersampling, SMOTE-style oversampling, and higher positive-class weights on the same time-series folds, using PR AUC plus recall at the target precision.
SMOTE created synthetic minority examples that fit noise in one-fold and hurt out-of-time folds; undersampling discarded too many transactions and made thresholds unstable.
Class weights preserved the original transaction distribution, making the score distribution more stable and threshold selection less sensitive to sampling artifacts.
Class weights also meant the serving-time score distribution matched what tuning assumed, which reduced drift surprises after deployment.
If the imbalance were truly extreme (e.g., <1:10,000 positives), we might need undersampling, anomaly detection, or a two-stage approach; class weights alone degrade.

topic: Metric choice, PR curve, and threshold selection
question_hint: You reported recall 0.62 at 90% precision and compared against 0.41. Why a PR curve instead of AUC, and how was that specific operating point chosen?
expected_points: With heavy class imbalance, ROC AUC was overly optimistic because the large true-negative group dominates; PR curve focuses on the positive class where the action is.

The operating point was chosen using a cost analysis: compare the cost of a false positive (manual review, customer friction, occasional false decline) against the cost of a false negative (the fraud amount).

The reported point is a threshold, not a magic model property; picking a more aggressive threshold might raise recall but was rejected because marginal false-positive cost outweighed the next fraud dollar caught.
The old 0.41 recall came from either a heuristic/threshold not tuned on the same cost tradeoff or a weaker model; the new XGBoost threshold was tuned on the PR curve's elbow.
Matched the business question by also looking at dollar-weighted recall, since losing a $5,000 transaction matters more than a $50 one; pure transaction-level metrics can mislead.

question_hint: You mention FastAPI, canary rollout and PSI drift pages. Walk me through what you treated as a signal to roll back during the canary, when offline metrics had already looked good.
expected_points: Defined rollback triggers before launch: p99 latency exceeding the 45ms SLO, error rate >0.1%, or a sharp drop in model score distribution consistency (PSI > 0.2) paired with business metric degradation.
PSI alone was not an automatic rollback; used it as a diagnostic and retrained if drift was gradual, but auto-rolled-back on latency/availability or sudden fraud-review workload spikes.
Canary sent a small fraction (e.g., 1-2%) of real traffic to the new model while the old model continued serving; compared both on live precision/alert rate, not just offline holdout.
Versioned model registry plus pre-built Kubernetes rollout config let the old model come back in under five minutes; the team practiced a drill, not just theorized it.
Learning: offline PR curves can hide feature-pipeline inconsistencies (e.g., missing Redis keys at serving time), so shadow/canary validation is what truly catches those bugs.

question_hint: Fraud offline metrics can flatter a model. If you had to prove this model actually reduced fraud losses in production, how would you set up an experiment or ramp to show causal impact?
expected_points: Would not just compare before/after due to seasonality and fraud adaptation; choose a randomized unit (transaction, card, or account) or a switchback/region design to minimize interference.
Primary metric would be net fraud loss per authorized transaction (or per $1000), with guardrail metrics like false-positive/decline rate, review workload, and customer complaints.
Watch for sample-ratio mismatch and verify the treatment/control split actually randomizes; fraud can propagate across cards, so consider clustering at the merchant or network level.
Fraud base rates are very low, so compute statistical power before starting; a one-week test will be too short — ask for a larger traffic share or longer ramp.
Would compare offline PR metrics as a prior but treat the online experiment as the proof; if offline pattern inverted online, investigate leakage or distribution shift rather than dismissing it.

topic: Confidence intervals and honest model evaluation
question_hint: The lift from recall 0.41 to 0.62 is big. How confident are you it wasn't luck or overfitting to one time period?
expected_points: Computed confidence intervals around the metric difference, e.g., paired bootstrap across transactions or McNemar's test, rather than reporting single point estimates.
Evaluated across multiple out-of-time folds from TimeSeriesSplit to see whether the lift was consistent in every fold or driven by one unusual month.
Kept a completely untouched final holdout period for the last check; threshold and model chosen on earlier validation folds were never tuned on that final holdout.
With 40M transactions, a tiny confidence interval can still be practically misleading; looked at dollar-weighted impact and not just per-transaction recall.
Lesson: every reported model comparison gets an uncertainty estimate and a statement of what was tuned on which split; this prevents fooling yourself and stakeholders.

topic: Communicating limitations to a non-technical stakeholder
question_hint: Imagine the fraud operations VP says: '62% recall means we still miss 38% of fraud — why can't your model catch all of it?' Walk me through your response.
expected_points: Explains the precision/recall tradeoff in business terms: catching more fraud (higher recall) would flood the review queue with false positives and risk declining legitimate customers; the PR curve shows this.
Translates 90% precision operationally: roughly 9 of 10 alerts are genuine fraud; using a more aggressive threshold to catch the last 38% would make false positives far more common than true misses.
Uses a simple dollar tradeoff to justify the operating point: cost of extra false positives > the fraud dollars recovered from low-score transactions.
Acknowledges the model's blind spots honestly: some fraud looks indistinguishable from normal activity or is too rare to learn; it will keep missing that until features or model evolve.

Proposes an action-oriented next step: if the VP wants fewer misses, we can either change the threshold and accept a higher false-positive cost, or invest in new features/feedback loops to lift the PR curve itself.

question_hint: Who asked you to build this and what exact target did you model? What made it the right definition for the business?
expected_points: Chose transaction-level confirmed fraud/chargeback as the positive event, not merely declined or disputed transactions.
Aligned the target with financial loss (fraud amount) rather than fraud count, since the business cared about dollar impact.
Defined a clear observation window and label delay to account for chargebacks arriving weeks after the transaction.
Checked with risk policy stakeholders before framing: there was an earlier ambiguity about whether to model on authorization or clearing data.
The final model predicted fraud probability per transaction, and the output was a score used in a rule-based decision.

question_hint: Walk me through the TimeSeriesSplit design. Why was random K-fold the wrong validation here, and what specific leakage did you have to prevent?
expected_points: Random K-fold overestimates performance because fraud patterns drift and random splits put future transactions in training, letting the model learn them.
Used calendar-ordered expanding or rolling windows (TimeSeriesSplit) where each training set only contains the past relative to the validation set.
Ensured no feature engineering on the validation fold: all aggregations like rolling averages or target encodings were computed per train split only.
Reported performance per fold to show stability across time periods, not just an average metric.
Mentioned an explicit check: the difference between random CV recall (e.g., 0.75) and time-series recall (0.62) highlighted how much leakage would have inflated results.

question_hint: You wrote that you chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. Walk me through the comparison and why class weights won.
expected_points: Compared under-sampling, over-sampling, SMOTE, and class weighting on the same TimeSeriesSplit folds, using the same evaluation metric (recall at fixed precision).
Under-sampling lost information by discarding many legitimate transactions; over-sampling led to overfitting on duplicate rows with diminished validation gains.
Class weights kept the full dataset, avoided synthetic data artifacts, and were simpler to implement in training and serving.
Tuned the class weight ratio via grid search on the validation metric.
Final choice supported the measured result: recall 0.62 at 90% precision, up from 0.41 with the old model.

question_hint: How did you decide to report recall at 90% precision instead of using the default 0.5 threshold?
expected_points: Did not use the default 0.5 threshold; it's meaningless when the base rate is extremely low.
Worked with product/finance to quantify the cost of false positives (review cost, false declines, customer friction) and false negatives (fraud loss).
Constructed a cost curve from the PR curve and picked the threshold that minimized total expected cost.
The 90% precision operating point was chosen because it kept reviewer efficiency and false-positive-friction at acceptable levels, while catching 62% of fraud.
Communicated the tradeoff clearly: there is no single best point, so I let the business cost structure determine it.

question_hint: After launch, what made you retrain or roll back? What signals were you watching?
expected_points: Monitored feature drift via PSI with alerting threshold at 0.2, per the resume claim.
Tracked online proxies: daily fraud decline rate, positive prediction ratio, and chargeback rate after label arrival.
Used canary releases for new model versions, comparing performance on a small fraction of traffic before a full rollout.
Had rollback automated through a versioned model registry so that if PSI exceeded threshold or precision dropped, could switch back in under five minutes.
Set a scheduled retraining cadence (e.g., weekly or monthly) as well as event-driven retraining when drift alerts fired.

question_hint: What measurable decision or business metric changed because of this model?
expected_points: Fraud detection recall increased from 0.41 to 0.62 at the same 90% precision, meaning more fraud caught without flooding the review queue.
This led to a measurable reduction in fraud losses or an increase in fraud dollars prevented per month.
The model replaced a rules-based heuristic as the primary decisioning layer for card transaction reviews.
The team moved from evaluating models on raw accuracy to using PR/cost curves, because accuracy was misleading at <2% fraud rate.
Operationally, the review team's workload stayed flat while more true-frauds were actioned.

question_hint: How would you run a fair experiment to prove this model beats the prior heuristic in production, given fraud labels arrive late?
expected_points: Proposed a two-step evaluation: offline replay on a held-out recent time period before anything online, then an online A/B test only if offline looked promising.

Designed the online A/B as a randomized unit at transaction level (or card level) with treatment (ML score) and control (old rules), pre-registering primary metrics like fraud loss per approved transaction and false positive rate.
Caused a delay: because chargebacks surface late, used a fixed observation window (e.g., 60 or 90 days) for both arms so label maturity is equal.
Calculated sample size and test duration using the expected lift and the low incidence rate, powering on fraud dollar loss not just on detection count.

Set guardrail metrics (authorization rate, decline rate, customer complaint rate) to catch collateral damage, and sunset the decision after statistical significance and practical relevance were reached.

question_hint: Walk me through the card-fraud scoring system from the raw transaction stream to the served prediction. Don't skip the batch pipeline—I want to know where features are computed and how the pieces talk to each other.
expected_points: Raw transactions land in object storage/streaming; Airflow batch jobs compute features over the 40M-transaction dataset and write precomputed features to Redis with TTL and appropriate keys.
Training pipeline reads historical labels with point-in-time joins, trains XGBoost offline, and registers a versioned artifact in a model registry.
FastAPI inference service on Kubernetes fetches features from Redis, calls the model, returns a score, and logs predictions plus feature values for monitoring.
Feature pipeline, model registry, and serving are decoupled, so model rollback can happen independently of code/feature changes.

topic: Class imbalance: class weights vs resampling, and metric choice
question_hint: Tell me more about the class-weights-vs-resampling ablation. What exactly did you compare, why did class weights win, and what metric made you call it a win?
expected_points: Compared class weights, random undersampling, and SMOTE using the same temporal validation split so synthetic-data choices didn't leak across folds.
Used PR curves and threshold tuning rather than AUC because fraud is rare and the business constraint was 90% precision.
Class weights achieved the target operating point—recall 0.62 at 90% precision, improved from 0.41—and generalized better across time folds.
The threshold was then re-checked on the most recent holdout window plus a simple cost model of false positives vs false negatives.

question_hint: Fraud models leak easily. What specific leakage paths were you protecting against, and why was TimeSeriesSplit the right validation? What would have happened with a random split?
expected_points: All features were point-in-time: aggregates for a transaction used only information available before that transaction's event time, not future windows.
Labels were applied after a fixed fraud-confirmation delay, and training data excluded transactions whose label window had not yet closed.
TimeSeriesSplit sorted by event time and trained only on past folds, so validation always came after training data.
A random split would let future transactions influence training, inflating offline PR/AUC and masking real-world temporal decay; leakage was caught by comparing offline metrics to online performance.

topic: Canary deployment, model registry, and fast rollback
question_hint: We need boring, fast rollbacks. You said canary rollout plus versioned registry plus rollback in under five minutes—walk me through the actual deployment and rollback flow. What signals make you abort a canary?
expected_points: Model artifacts are stored immutably with version/hash in a registry; Kubernetes canary deployment or service-mesh traffic split sends a small fraction to the new model while the old version stays live.
Canary monitors error rate, p99 latency, throughput, prediction distribution/PSI, and delayed labels; if any signal crosses a threshold, the canary is automatically aborted.
Rollback resets traffic to the previous version via the registry, reusing the prior artifact and deployment spec, which takes under five minutes.
A key lesson: feature schema and model version must be checked together, because rolling back the model alone is unsafe if the feature store contract has changed.

topic: Redis feature store and request batching for latency
question_hint: You cut inference p99 from 180ms to 45ms. What was actually slow before, why did Redis and batching fix it, and what new problems did they introduce?
expected_points: The bottleneck was per-request feature computation and multiple remote database roundtrips, not the XGBoost tree evaluation itself.

A Redis feature store precomputed features and allowed fetching all needed values in a single pipelined call, while model-call batching turned many single-row predictions into one vectorized predict call.
Measured p99 dropped from 180ms to 45ms without changing model outputs, since the same feature values were served.

Tradeoffs included feature freshness/TTL, Redis memory cost, cache consistency, and extra latency from micro-batching under low traffic; these were handled with TTL tuning, load tests, and careful timeout/backpressure settings.

question_hint: You built feature drift monitoring pages and used PSI > 0.2. What exactly is being monitored, why 0.2, and what is the runbook when the page goes red?
expected_points: Monitored per-feature PSI between a recent sliding window and the training distribution, plus missingness, freshness, and aggregate population stability over cards/accounts.
The 0.2 threshold was chosen after looking at historical feature volatility and the model's sensitivity to drift, not picked arbitrarily; it balanced alerting on real shift against alert fatigue.
A red page triggered investigation of the upstream feature pipeline, data sources, and any recent model deployment; broad PSI shifts often indicated data bugs, not just a change in fraud patterns.
If drift coincided with a recent canary, rollback was considered; otherwise, delayed-label model performance was checked to decide whether retraining was needed.

topic: Reproducibility, testing, and CI/CD for ML pipelines
question_hint: If I want to redeploy this same system six months from now, what ensures I get the same model, the same features, and no surprises? How did you test changes in CI?
expected_points: Training and serving run in containers with pinned dependencies; data snapshots and feature definitions are versioned, and each training run records config, hyperparameters, data version, metrics, and artifact hash.
CI runs unit tests on feature logic plus data validation, and a model regression gate compares new candidates to the champion on a golden temporal holdout before anything can merge.
Serving is tested with contract/schema tests using recorded real feature vectors, so a new model artifact cannot be deployed against an incompatible feature schema.

The platform-style takeaway is that these pieces—containerized pipelines, versioned datasets, registry, and CI gates—are what make ML deployments reproducible enough to be a paved road for other teams.

topic: Failure modes, capacity, and cost controls
question_hint: Let's stress this system. Pick one component—Redis, the inference deployment, or the feature pipeline—and tell me how it can fail, how you'd detect it, and what you'd do to keep fraud scoring reliable and cost under control.
expected_points: If Redis fails or evicts keys, serving should fail closed for fraud review or fall back to a slower authoritative source with a circuit breaker; replication and a warm-up plan prevent a cold-cache thundering herd after recovery.

Kubernetes inference needs HPA based on p99 latency and request rate, plus an error budget; capacity tests determine replica counts, and cost levers include right-sizing, spot instances for stateless work, and watching batch-size/feature count per request.

Feature pipeline failures are detected by scheduled DAG alerts and freshness/late-data monitors; stale or missing features should block deployment or trigger an explicit degraded mode, never silently score with zeros.

Cost reasoning starts with QPS, features per request, Redis memory per key for the TTL window, and CPU per request; comparing that against a local cache alternative shows whether the Redis feature store spend is justified.

question_hint: You mentioned validating with TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. Walk me through your evaluation design for the fraud model — where could leakage have come in if you had not been careful, and how did you handle it?
expected_points: Used a chronological split: train on transactions before a cutoff, validate on an adjacent window, and test on a later window; random cross-validation would leak future transaction patterns into training.
Ensured point-in-time correctness: every feature at scoring time used only data available before that transaction, so aggregates were computed over trailing windows with no lookahead on the label.
Recognized fraud labels are delayed, so a gap was left between training and validation windows to avoid labels that were not yet known at the prediction time.
The reported headline numbers (recall 0.62 at 90% precision) came from this time-series holdout, not from random CV, so they reflected real future performance.

topic: Class imbalance, resampling vs class weights, and threshold selection
question_hint: For the fraud model, you used class weights over resampling and tuned threshold on PR curves. Why did that win, and what did the ablation actually show?
expected_points: Compared class weights against SMOTE and random undersampling on the same time-series split; class weights performed comparably or better on PR AUC while preserving all original examples.
Resampling is brittle at low fraud prevalence: synthetic minority samples can resemble legitimate patterns and add false positives, while undersampling can discard useful legitimate transactions.
Ablation varied the class-weight ratio systematically and evaluated with recall at target precision on the validation window, not just AUC.
Selected the decision threshold after training by moving along the PR curve to hit 90% precision; that tradeoff produced recall 0.62 versus 0.41 in the previous system.
Considered the business cost of false positives (alerts) versus false negatives (missed fraud), not only a statistical metric.

question_hint: Walk me through serving this model behind FastAPI on Kubernetes. You mentioned a canary rollout — what was the exact mechanism and how did you decide when a new model was safe to promote?
expected_points: The FastAPI model server was containerized with pinned dependencies and deployed as a Kubernetes Deployment; the image tag was tied to the model registry version.
Canary was done by running two co-existing model deployments and shifting a small percentage (for example, 5–10%) of production traffic to the new version using ingress/service-mesh weighted routing.
Health checks included readiness and liveness probes plus error-rate and p99-latency monitoring; promotion happened only after a quiet observation period, not just because the pod started.
Rollback was fast because the old artifact still existed in the versioned model registry; reverting meant shifting traffic back to the previous deployment or running kubectl rollout undo.
Canary was chosen over blue-green because it limited the blast radius and still surfaced model-specific problems like feature drift on live traffic.

topic: Redis feature store, request batching, and new failure modes
question_hint: You reduced p99 from 180ms to 45ms by moving feature lookups to Redis and batching model calls. What had been slow, and what new failure modes did you introduce?
expected_points: Latency came from per-request feature computation and repeated database/join work; moving stable computed features into Redis made lookups millisecond-level.
Made model inference batchable by combining multiple transaction lookup keys into one XGBoost prediction call, improving throughput and reducing per-request overhead.
Considered a local in-process cache but rejected it because model replicas were not in sync; a central Redis feature store provided consistency and a single cache to warm and backfill.

New failure modes included Redis cache misses on cold keys, stale aggregates when upstream feature jobs lagged, and hotspot keys during traffic spikes; mitigated with fallbacks, TTLs/freshness checks, and Redis clustering/replication.
Measured p99 and p999 after the change, because request batching can hide tail latency and queuing effects.

topic: Feature drift monitoring and rollback playbook
question_hint: You built drift monitoring on PSI over 0.2 and a five-minute rollback. What exactly did you monitor, why 0.2 as the threshold, and what actually happens during a rollback?
expected_points: PSI was computed per feature between the training/expected distribution and a rolling production window; the dashboard flagged any feature with PSI > 0.2 and showed which feature or segment drifted.
0.2 was a deliberate threshold: PSI under 0.1 is considered small, 0.1–0.25 moderate, so 0.2 triggered before severe degradation but was tuned to avoid noisy alerts.

Rollback was driven by a versioned model registry: model artifacts and container images were immutable, and the deploy config referenced a specific version, so reverting was a config change plus kubectl apply.
The runbook stated that unambiguous drift on high-impact features triggered rollback, while ambiguous drift escalated to on-call review first.
Also watched label/concept drift when fraud labels became available, because not every feature shift is bad — some shifts are real changes in the world and the model may still be valid.

topic: Reproducibility, CI/CD, and testing for ML deployments
question_hint: The team expects ML deployment to be boring and reproducible. For this fraud model, what would you consider the minimum standard for CI/CD and testing before a model can be deployed?
expected_points: Automated unit tests for feature transformations, integration tests on a small slice of transactions, and container smoke tests that exercise the FastAPI endpoint.
Training is reproducible: the same code commit, input data version, config, and hyperparameters regenerate the same model artifact and eval metrics.
CI runs the full training plus evaluation on every merge or at least nightly and enforces regression gates, such as recall-at-target-precision not dropping below the committed baseline.

CD deploys to staging using the same Helm charts/Terraform as production; after staging validation it starts a canary, and promotion goes through the same pipeline used by every model on the platform.
Dependency and infra fingerprinting: container images pinned by digest, Python and system packages locked, and Kubernetes manifests/Helm charts versioned to make rollback a first-class operation.

topic: Capacity planning, autoscaling, and cost controls
question_hint: Suppose a partner team triples its request traffic on this fraud-scoring service overnight. How would you make sure the serving platform scales, and what cost controls kick in?
expected_points: Use Kubernetes HPA on request rate and latency plus cluster autoscaler for node capacity; HPA min/max is informed by load tests that show each replica's sustainable throughput.
Model the bottleneck: if Redis feature lookups become the constraint, scale the Redis cluster or add read replicas; if inference is the constraint, increase model replicas and batch size.
Set CPU/memory requests and limits to match the actual serving profile so the cluster autoscaler does not waste nodes; use per-team cost labels and budget alerts.
Consider over-provisioning during planned launches because autoscaling has a warm-up lag; for unexpected spikes, active readiness and fast scaling from surplus node pools guard the SLO.
Balance cost and reliability: latency-critical scoring may need on-demand nodes, while non-latency-sensitive feature precompute can run on spot instances with interruption tolerance.

topic: Problem framing, baseline, and success metric
question_hint: You said you built a card-fraud scoring model on 40M transactions. What exactly were you optimizing, what was the baseline you compared against, and how did you frame the problem to make the project tractable?
expected_points: Clearly states the business problem: score each transaction in real time to detect fraud while limiting false declines; fraud is a tiny fraction of transactions.
Names the baseline (e.g., existing rule engine or logistic regression) and says the XGBoost model was compared to it on the same temporal split.
Explains why accuracy is a useless metric here and why they chose precision-recall / expected cost; cites recall 0.62 at 90% precision vs 0.41 for baseline.
Mentions how confirmed fraud was defined and bounded by a time window (e.g., chargeback within 30/60 days), which connects to label construction.
Describes the project scope as ranking transactions and then picking a threshold, not just building a classifier.

question_hint: Your resume says you used TimeSeriesSplit to prevent leakage. Walk me through the validation setup you designed and what leakage you were guarding against.
expected_points: Explains why random K-fold cross-validation is inappropriate for transactional fraud data because transactions from the same account/merchant/time window leak information across folds.
Describes a temporal split: sort by transaction timestamp, train on past data, validate on future data, possibly using an expanding or rolling window.
Mentions purging or adding a gap between train and test to avoid labels from the test period being constructed using events that occur after the prediction time.
States that features were computed only from data available at scoring time and that target/outcome windows did not overlap with training features.
Emphasizes that they used the same split consistently for baselines, ablations, and hyperparameter tuning to keep comparisons fair.

question_hint: You mentioned choosing class weights over resampling after an ablation. How did you run that ablation, and what evidence convinced you that class weights were the right approach?
expected_points: Names the resampling alternatives they tested, e.g., random undersampling of the majority class, SMOTE/oversampling, and class weights using scale_pos_weight in XGBoost.
Says they compared all methods on the same TimeSeriesSplit and evaluated on recall at the target precision (90%), not just AUC or F1.
Reports that class weights were comparable or better on PR-based metrics and were also cheaper/faster to train; resampling increased risk of overfitting or introduced synthetic patterns.
Shows awareness that the natural class ratio is not the same as the optimal weight because a false negative is much more expensive than a false positive; they weighted fraud more heavily.
Mentions an operational criterion: class weights integrated naturally into training and did not complicate the serving pipeline.

topic: Threshold tuning and PR vs. ROC
question_hint: How did you go from a trained model to the deployed threshold that gave recall 0.62 at 90% precision? What were the tradeoffs, and why PR curves instead of ROC?
expected_points: Explains that they treated the threshold as a separate decision step, selecting it to satisfy an operational constraint, e.g., 90% precision to cap false declines.

Walks through the cost tradeoff: false positives irritate customers and cost approval fees/interchange, while false negatives directly cause fraud losses; picked the operating point by estimated dollar cost.
States they used PR curves because ROC is misleading under severe class imbalance and doesn't directly show precision at feasible recall levels.
Mentions that they calibrated predicted probabilities (e.g., isotonic regression) before thresholding so that the 0.9 threshold was meaningful.
Notes that the threshold was re-evaluated over time as fraud prevalence changed, and monitoring included metrics like decline rate and chargeback rate.

topic: Complexity and model selection — did the best idea earn its complexity?
question_hint: XGBoost is a strong but somewhat standard choice. What other modeling approaches did you consider, and what made XGBoost the winner? How did you decide that the complexity of any alternative was justified?
expected_points: Lists alternatives such as deep neural networks (e.g., MLP or tabular transformers), gradient boosting variants, and perhaps logistic regression; explains why each was considered.
States they prototyped a deeper model but found it did not improve test-set PR metrics (e.g., recall at 90% precision) enough to justify added serving complexity and latency.
Talks about feature engineering rather than model class as the main source of lift; e.g., velocity features, merchant risk, device signals, and account age were validated by ablations.
Mentions they used feature importance and time-series validation to drop features that only helped on random splits but not on temporal splits, avoiding overfitting.
Concludes with the lesson: start with the strongest simple baseline, measure against it, and only add complexity when it buys a meaningful metric improvement under realistic constraints.

topic: Online evaluation, canary rollout, and falsifiability
question_hint: You reported a strong offline improvement—recall from 0.41 to 0.62. But offline metrics can lie. How did you validate that the model was actually better online, and what would have convinced you that your result was wrong?
expected_points: Describes shadow-mode scoring or a canary A/B test where the new model's scores were logged against live outcomes without immediately affecting all traffic.
Identifies online guardrail metrics: fraud capture rate, false positive/decline rate, customer complaint rate, and maybe late chargebacks; notes chargeback confirmation requires a delay window.
Mentioned the PSI drift monitoring and the rollback trigger (PSI > 0.2); if drift or decline rate spiked, the canary was cut off and the old model restarted.

Shows scientific honesty by naming confounders—fraud patterns shift, canary traffic may not be perfectly representative, and offline metrics don't reflect user friction—so they did not treat the offline lift as proof.
Can describe the rule they predefined for calling the deployment a success: e.g., recall/realized fraud capture at the target precision held for two weeks without regression in guardrail metrics.

topic: Reproducibility and handing off to others
question_hint: Your job is to turn a research prototype into something others on the team can build on. What did you do to make the fraud model reproducible—so another scientist or engineer could recreate your experiments and deploy from your notes?
expected_points: Mentions using experiment tracking to log dataset version, split definition, hyperparameters, and evaluation results, so every model card corresponds to a reproducible run.
Describes code structure: versioned training pipeline, configuration files, and a model registry with immutable artifacts; avoids relying on ad-hoc notebooks.
Explains that metrics, thresholds, and data transforms were stored with the model artifact, and the training script could be rerun end-to-end on the frozen dataset.
Mentions writing up the findings: baseline comparison, ablation results, limitations, and known failure modes, so the next person understands what was tried and why.
Demonstrates good practice by saying they tested rollback and deployment playbooks and documented them, not just the model.

question_hint: Walk me through the operational context: what were you replacing, what real-world constraint drove the model design, and what was the baseline to beat?
expected_points: Stated the goal: score every card transaction in near real-time to catch fraud while keeping false positives acceptable.
Identified the incumbent as a rules-based engine or simple model with recall 0.41 at 90% precision on the same problem.
Articulated the 90% precision business constraint (e.g., customer friction, review cost, false-positive cost).
Explained why XGBoost was chosen initially but benchmarked against a simpler linear model to justify the complexity.

question_hint: You mentioned you chose class weights over resampling after an ablation. What exactly did you compare, and how did you judge which was better?
expected_points: Compared class-weighted XGBoost against random undersampling and SMOTE while keeping the same validation folds and metric definitions.
Evaluated on the test set with its natural (imbalanced) class distribution, not a balanced subset.
Found class weights matched or beat resampling on precision-recall while preserving training speed and avoiding synthetic-data artifacts.
Separated model training from threshold tuning, then calibrated the operating threshold on the PR curve per fold.

question_hint: You said TimeSeriesSplit prevented leakage. Walk me through how you constructed your splits and the specific types of leakage you had to guard against.
expected_points: Used expanding-window chronological splits: train on older blocks, validate/test on later blocks, never shuffled randomly.
Computed all features point-in-time so they used only information available before the transaction timestamp.
Ensured no resampling or feature encoding was fitted before splitting; any label-derived statistics were strictly out-of-time.
Hardened against label leakage caused by fraud labels maturing later (e.g., used a label lookback window before evaluating).

question_hint: From 0.41 to 0.62 recall at 90% precision: how do you know that lift is real and not luck on one split?
expected_points: Did not rely on a single split; used multiple contiguous time-series hold-out windows or expanding-window folds.
Applied paired bootstrap or a proper significance test (e.g., McNemar, approximate binomial) at the chosen threshold.
Reported a confidence interval around the recall improvement that excluded zero.
Handled time-series non-independence by using block-bootstrap or evaluating across multiple served weeks in production.

topic: Complexity that did not pay off
question_hint: A senior scientist is expected to know when not to add complexity. What more complex alternatives did you try on the fraud model, and how did you confirm they weren't worth it?
expected_points: Mentioned a concrete alternative tried, e.g., a deep sequence model or a gradient-boosted model with added stacked features.
Compared it against the XGBoost baseline with identical features and fold structure; the gain in PR AUC was within noise or marginal.
Weighed the added serving and debugging complexity against a few basis points of improvement and rejected it.
Kept the simpler model because interpretability mattered for risk/compliance teams and for fast rollback.

question_hint: Offline results can lie. What specific evidence would have made you reverse an earlier conclusion? How did you decide the canary deployment was actually worth keeping?
expected_points: Pre-registered the expected operational metrics: real-time precision/recall proxy, fraud/dispute rate, and the decision threshold.
Tracked feature drift (PSI > 0.2 on key model inputs) to detect train/serve skew before it hurt performance.
Set rollback triggers: a drop in observed precision below the offline target, an abnormal fraud rate, or a latency SLO breach.
Shadow-scored the new model against the previous one before the canary to confirm the expected lift on live traffic.

topic: Label definition and data quality traps
question_hint: Fraud labels are rarely clean. How did you define ground truth for your 40M transactions, and what biases could that introduce into your reported 0.62/0.41 numbers?
expected_points: Explained label source and timing: confirmed fraud from chargebacks/disputes, but recognize unreported fraud creates false negatives.
Described the label-maturity problem: transactions need a sufficient observation window to know if they become fraudulent.
Controlled for this by evaluating on older transactions where labels were mature and by using a consistent label window across models.
Acknowledged that precision at '90%' can be optimistic if disputed-but-not-fraud transactions are counted as positives or excluded from evaluation.

question_hint: The job involves writing up findings so others can build on them. How did you hand off this model and its evaluation so your teammates could reproduce or update it?
expected_points: Versioned the model in a registry with training config, data snapshot, exact feature definitions, and evaluation code.
Documented the ablation that led to class weights over resampling, the metric file, and the decision thresholds.
Recorded the TimeSeriesSplit scheme and hyperparameters in an experiment tracker (e.g., MLflow/W&B) to allow exact reproduction.
Built a regression gate in CI: a golden set of past transactions with expected metrics so future changes don't silently degrade.
Created a lightweight design note explaining the operating trade-off and the evidence behind it.
